A1.justification: These are identifiable versions of the same research work, with v2 substantially extending its scope. Both PDFs provide sufficient text, equations, figures and tables for comparison, including v2's Appendices A-D; v1 has no separate appendices.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original skip-list insertion and query experiments on synthetic distributions, CAIDA traffic and AOL queries.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report skip-list experiments and original KD-tree evaluations on synthetic data, a 3D mesh, multilingual n-grams and neuron activity.

M1.justification: v2 introduces KD-tree construction using probability-based axis splits, frequent negative-query points and balanced construction for low-frequency data. Its skip-list algorithm replaces the fixed level cap with termination at an empty level, and v1's separate two-list robustness construction is removed.

E1.justification: v2 retains synthetic skip-list, CAIDA and AOL coverage while adding multidimensional point lookup on synthetic distributions, Stanford Lucy surface samples, Google 2-5grams across multiple languages, and 30-cell neuronal activity vectors. These introduce substantial new domains and input requirements.

E2.justification: Traditional KD trees become an additional evaluated comparator throughout the new KD-tree experiments, including Tables 3-4. The existing vanilla skip-list comparator is retained, often renamed classic. The separate BST-versus-standard-skip-list experiment is contextual evidence, not a BST comparison against the proposed method.

E3.justification: New KD-tree protocols measure query depth alongside timing, use 4096 points and 16384 queries for 3D sweeps, and test 10000 points with one million queries across dimensions 1-40. Lucy uses separately sampled construction and query data. The retained CAIDA chronological splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's skewness and CAIDA temporal-stability analyses, v2 adds KD-tree sensitivity tests for additive and multiplicative prediction noise, random versus spatially smooth frequencies, and dimensionality. Figure 8 also adds a construction-cost comparison between standard BSTs and skip lists.

E5.justification: v2 specifies 32 repetitions and reports medians of average query depths for the KD-tree sweeps in Figures 4-5 and 11. v1 provides no corresponding repeated-run reporting. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or variability estimates; this does not establish increased repetition of retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial KD-tree results: learned versus traditional query depths are 15.1 versus 17.6 on Lucy and 14.9 versus 23.7 on neuron activity. Tables 3-4 add dimensionality and n-gram results, with Table 3 also showing higher construction costs. Synthetic skip-list timing curves change between v1 Figures 1-2 and v2 Figures 6-7, although Tables 1-2 retain their values.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix C add KD-tree depth, entropy, lower-bound and noisy-oracle statements and proofs. For skip lists, v2 adds the probabilistic height argument in Lemma B.6 and Theorem 2.1, and tightens the noise assumption from beta < 1/(2n) to beta < alpha/(4n), matching the earlier proof. Most existing entropy arguments are relocated.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions extend nearly-factor-two optimality, tolerance of approximate predictions and robustness claims from skip lists to both skip lists and KD trees. Multidimensional search and its theoretical and empirical treatment become central contributions absent from v1.

C2.justification: The explanations of skip-list gains and CAIDA oracle stability are retained. v2 adds explanations of why the exponential multidimensional search space motivates truncating rare queries, why frequent negative queries need special treatment, and why BST rebalancing contributes to construction overhead.

D1.justification: v2 adds KD-specific hardware and operating-system specifications, mesh sampling and spatial binning instructions, n-gram word-index representations, and 20 ms binning of neuronal activity. New data-source references accompany these experiments. The original skip-list hardware and CAIDA prediction-construction details remain.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes concurrent work by Zeynali et al. and develops its relationship to Lin et al.'s learned BSTs. Appendix A substantially expands positioning around learned B-trees, static optimality, self-improving algorithms and self-adjusting structures. The earlier S3, Phast and Jellyfish discussion and citations are removed.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and its abstract, introduction and algorithm motivation are substantially rewritten. Most skip-list proofs move into Appendix B, and synthetic/AOL experiments move into Appendix D. The standalone predictor-robustness section is reorganized, the conclusion is removed, and KD-tree material becomes a main section.

P2.justification: Existing skip-list charts are redrawn with larger labels and revised axis presentation, and many displays move between the main text and appendix. v2 adds KD-tree heatmaps, the BST construction chart and Tables 3-4. Figures 5 and 11 partly redisplay the same KD-tree parameter-sweep results.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical breadth, experimental disclosure and research positioning, and corrects the skip-list noise-threshold mismatch. However, its new central KD-tree guarantees have unresolved support gaps: Lemma C.1 assumes exact half-mass splits although Algorithm 2 only selects the closest split, and Lemma 3.4's proof uses a stricter noise bound than its statement. These theoretical issues coexist with substantial empirical benefits, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
